claim: The TCR extracellular (EC) domain attains tilt angles relative to the membrane normal that range from 15° to 55°.
source: We find that the TCR extracellular (EC) domain is highly variable in its orientation by attaining tilt angles relative to the membrane normal that range from 15° to 55°.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from atomistic molecular dynamics simulations showing the distribution of tilt angles.

claim: The tilt angle of the TCR EC domain is coupled to a rotation of the domain.
source: The tilt angle of the TCR EC domain is both coupled to a rotation of the domain and to characteristic changes throughout the TCR – CD3 complex, in particular in the EC interactions of the Cβ FG loop of the TCR, as well as in the orientation of transmembrane helices.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data showing correlation between tilt and rotation angles.

claim: The tilt angle of the TCR EC domain is coupled to characteristic changes in the EC interactions of the Cβ FG loop.
source: The tilt angle of the TCR EC domain is both coupled to a rotation of the domain and to characteristic changes throughout the TCR – CD3 complex, in particular in the EC interactions of the Cβ FG loop of the TCR, as well as in the orientation of transmembrane helices.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data showing changes in Cβ FG loop contacts with tilt angle.

claim: The tilt angle of the TCR EC domain is coupled to changes in the orientation of transmembrane helices.
source: The tilt angle of the TCR EC domain is both coupled to a rotation of the domain and to characteristic changes throughout the TCR – CD3 complex, in particular in the EC interactions of the Cβ FG loop of the TCR, as well as in the orientation of transmembrane helices.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data showing changes in TM helix inclination angles with TCR EC domain tilt.

claim: T cells recognize peptide antigens presented by major histocompatibility complexes (MHC) on apposing cell surfaces as a central step in the initiation of adaptive immune responses.
source: T cells recognize peptide antigens presented by major histocompatibility complexes (MHC) on apposing cell surfaces as a central step in the initiation of adaptive immune responses (Rossjohn et al., 2015; Smith-Garvin et al., 2009; Dustin, 2014; Pettmann et al., 2018; Belardi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The heterodimeric TCRαβ contains the binding site for recognizing peptide antigens.
source: In this complex, the heterodimeric TCRαβ contains the binding site for recognizing peptide antigens, and the associated CD3εδ and CD3εγ heterodimers and the CD3ζζ homodimer contain the intracellular signaling motifs that transmit antigen binding to T cell activation (Wucherpfennig et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The CD3εδ and CD3εγ heterodimers and the CD3ζζ homodimer contain the intracellular signaling motifs that transmit antigen binding to T cell activation.
source: In this complex, the heterodimeric TCRαβ contains the binding site for recognizing peptide antigens, and the associated CD3εδ and CD3εγ heterodimers and the CD3ζζ homodimer contain the intracellular signaling motifs that transmit antigen binding to T cell activation (Wucherpfennig et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The stoichiometry of the TCR-CD3 complex has been known for nearly two decades.
source: While this stoichiometry of the complex has been known for nearly two decades (Call et al., 2002), the structure of the TCR – CD3 complex remained a puzzling problem (Fernandes et al., 2012; Birnbaum et al., 2014; Natarajan et al., 2016) that has only been recently solved by Dong et al., 2019 with cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Call et al., 2002.

claim: The structure of the TCR – CD3 complex was solved by Dong et al., 2019 with cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM).
source: While this stoichiometry of the complex has been known for nearly two decades (Call et al., 2002), the structure of the TCR – CD3 complex remained a puzzling problem (Fernandes et al., 2012; Birnbaum et al., 2014; Natarajan et al., 2016) that has only been recently solved by Dong et al., 2019 with cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2019.

claim: Dong et al. expressed all proteins of the TCR-CD3 complex in cultured cells.
source: To determine the structure, Dong et al. expressed all proteins of the complex in cultured cells, replaced the cell membrane around the assembled TCR – CD3 complex by the detergent digitonin, and stabilized the interactions between the extracellular (EC) domains of TCRαβ, CD3εδ and CD3εγ by chemical crosslinking.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used by Dong et al., cited in the text.

claim: Dong et al. replaced the cell membrane around the assembled TCR – CD3 complex by the detergent digitonin.
source: To determine the structure, Dong et al. expressed all proteins of the complex in cultured cells, replaced the cell membrane around the assembled TCR – CD3 complex by the detergent digitonin, and stabilized the interactions between the extracellular (EC) domains of TCRαβ, CD3εδ and CD3εγ by chemical crosslinking.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used by Dong et al., cited in the text.

claim: Dong et al. stabilized the interactions between the extracellular (EC) domains of TCRαβ, CD3εδ and CD3εγ by chemical crosslinking.
source: To determine the structure, Dong et al. expressed all proteins of the complex in cultured cells, replaced the cell membrane around the assembled TCR – CD3 complex by the detergent digitonin, and stabilized the interactions between the extracellular (EC) domains of TCRαβ, CD3εδ and CD3εγ by chemical crosslinking.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used by Dong et al., cited in the text.

claim: In the cryo-EM structure, the EC domains of CD3εδ and CD3εγ are both in contact with TCRαβ and with each other.
source: In the cryo-EM structure, the EC domains of CD3εδ and CD3εγ are both in contact with TCRαβ and with each other (see Figure 1), which explains the cooperative binding of CD3εδ and CD3εγ to TCRαβ observed in chain assembly (Call et al., 2002), mutational (Kuhns and Davis, 2007; Kuhns and Davis, 2012), and NMR experiments (He et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the cryo-EM structure and Figure 1.

claim: The contact arrangement of CD3εδ and CD3εγ with TCRαβ explains the cooperative binding of CD3εδ and CD3εγ to TCRαβ observed in chain assembly, mutational, and NMR experiments.
source: In the cryo-EM structure, the EC domains of CD3εδ and CD3εγ are both in contact with TCRαβ and with each other (see Figure 1), which explains the cooperative binding of CD3εδ and CD3εγ to TCRαβ observed in chain assembly (Call et al., 2002), mutational (Kuhns and Davis, 2007; Kuhns and Davis, 2012), and NMR experiments (He et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from structural data and citations to experimental observations.

claim: The DE loop of the membrane-proximal constant domain Cα of TCRα is in contact with the CD3εδ EC domain.
source: As indicated by mutational experiments (Kuhns and Davis, 2007; Kuhns and Davis, 2012), the DE loop of the membrane-proximal constant domain Cα of TCRα is in contact with the CD3εδ EC domain, and the CC' loop of the constant domain Cβ of TCRβ is in contact with both the CD3εγ and CD3εδ EC domains in the assembled TCR – CD3 complex (see Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mutational experiments and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The CC' loop of the constant domain Cβ of TCRβ is in contact with both the CD3εγ and CD3εδ EC domains in the assembled TCR – CD3 complex.
source: As indicated by mutational experiments (Kuhns and Davis, 2007; Kuhns and Davis, 2012), the DE loop of the membrane-proximal constant domain Cα of TCRα is in contact with the CD3εδ EC domain, and the CC' loop of the constant domain Cβ of TCRβ is in contact with both the CD3εγ and CD3εδ EC domains in the assembled TCR – CD3 complex (see Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mutational experiments and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The Cβ FG loop has been suggested to play a key role in T cell activation.
source: The Cβ FG loop, for example, has been suggested to play a key role in T cell activation (Kim et al., 2010; Touma et al., 2006), but exhibits only rather limited contacts with CD3εγ in the cryo-EM structure (see Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2010 and Touma et al., 2006.

claim: The Cβ FG loop exhibits only rather limited contacts with CD3εγ in the cryo-EM structure.
source: The Cβ FG loop, for example, has been suggested to play a key role in T cell activation (Kim et al., 2010; Touma et al., 2006), but exhibits only rather limited contacts with CD3εγ in the cryo-EM structure (see Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 showing the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The simulations have a cumulative simulation length of 120 μs.
source: In this article, we investigate the structural and orientational variability of the membrane-embedded TCR – CD3 complex in extensive, atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with a cumulative simulation length of 120 μs.
evidence: This claim describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: Significantly more residues of TCRαβ are involved in EC domain contacts along the simulation trajectories compared to the cryo-EM structure.
source: Compared to the cryo-EM structure, significantly more residues of TCRαβ are involved in EC domain contacts along our simulation trajectories, in particular in the Cβ FG loop, and notably also in the variable domain Vα of the TCRα chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data comparing to the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The Cβ FG loop is involved in significantly more EC domain contacts in the simulations compared to the cryo-EM structure.
source: Compared to the cryo-EM structure, significantly more residues of TCRαβ are involved in EC domain contacts along our simulation trajectories, in particular in the Cβ FG loop, and notably also in the variable domain Vα of the TCRα chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data comparing to the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The variable domain Vα of the TCRα chain is involved in significantly more EC domain contacts in the simulations compared to the cryo-EM structure.
source: Compared to the cryo-EM structure, significantly more residues of TCRαβ are involved in EC domain contacts along our simulation trajectories, in particular in the Cβ FG loop, and notably also in the variable domain Vα of the TCRα chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data comparing to the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The tilt of the TCRαβ EC domain is coupled to characteristic changes in the overall structure of the TCR – CD3 complex.
source: The tilt of the TCRαβ EC domain is both coupled to a rotation of the domain and to characteristic changes in the overall structure of the TCR – CD3 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data showing correlations between tilt angle and structural changes.

claim: The structural changes associated with TCRαβ EC domain tilt include a clear decrease of contacts in the Cβ FG loop with increasing tilt angle.
source: These structural changes include a clear decrease of contacts in the Cβ FG loop and an increase of contacts in the Vα domain with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain, as well as changes in the orientation of the transmembrane (TM) helices of the TCRα and CD3γ chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data showing contact changes with tilt angle.

claim: The structural changes associated with TCRαβ EC domain tilt include an increase of contacts in the Vα domain with increasing tilt angle.
source: These structural changes include a clear decrease of contacts in the Cβ FG loop and an increase of contacts in the Vα domain with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain, as well as changes in the orientation of the transmembrane (TM) helices of the TCRα and CD3γ chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data showing contact changes with tilt angle.

claim: The structural changes associated with TCRαβ EC domain tilt include changes in the orientation of the transmembrane (TM) helices of the TCRα and CD3γ chain.
source: These structural changes include a clear decrease of contacts in the Cβ FG loop and an increase of contacts in the Vα domain with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain, as well as changes in the orientation of the transmembrane (TM) helices of the TCRα and CD3γ chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data showing TM helix orientation changes with tilt angle.

claim: The concerted motions of the membrane-embedded TCR – CD3 complex provide atomistic insights on conformational changes of the complex in response to tilt-inducing forces on antigen-bound TCRs.
source: The concerted motions of the membrane-embedded TCR – CD3 complex revealed in our simulations provide atomistic insights on conformational changes of the complex in response to tilt-inducing forces on antigen-bound TCRs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the simulation results about force-induced conformational changes.

claim: The simulations were conducted with the Amber99SB-ILDN protein force field.
source: We have conducted these simulations with the Amber99SB-ILDN protein force field (Lindorff-Larsen et al., 2010) and the Amber Lipid14 membrane force field (Dickson et al., 2014) at a simulation temperature of 30°C on graphics processing units (GPUs).
evidence: This claim describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: The simulations were conducted with the Amber Lipid14 membrane force field.
source: We have conducted these simulations with the Amber99SB-ILDN protein force field (Lindorff-Larsen et al., 2010) and the Amber Lipid14 membrane force field (Dickson et al., 2014) at a simulation temperature of 30°C on graphics processing units (GPUs).
evidence: This claim describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: The simulations were conducted at a simulation temperature of 30°C.
source: We have conducted these simulations with the Amber99SB-ILDN protein force field (Lindorff-Larsen et al., 2010) and the Amber Lipid14 membrane force field (Dickson et al., 2014) at a simulation temperature of 30°C on graphics processing units (GPUs).
evidence: This claim describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the TCR – CD3 protein complex was embedded in a membrane composed of 456 POPC lipids and 114 cholesterol molecules.
source: The simulation trajectories start from initial system conformations in which the cryo-EM structure of the TCR – CD3 protein complex is embedded in a membrane composed of 456 POPC lipids and 114 cholesterol molecules.
evidence: This claim describes the computational system setup.

claim: The orientational and conformational ensembles sampled by the 120 trajectories equilibrate within the first 0.5 μs of the simulation trajectories.
source: We find that the orientational and conformational ensembles sampled by the 120 trajectories equilibrate within the first 0.5 μs of the simulation trajectories (see Materials and methods) and, therefore, focus on the second 0.5 μs of the MD simulation trajectories in our analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation data showing equilibration.

claim: The contact maps include all residue-residue contacts that occur in the simulations with a probability larger than 0.5%.
source: The contact maps of Figure 2 include all residue-residue contacts that occur in the simulations with a probability larger than 0.5%.
evidence: This claim describes the analysis method for contact maps.

claim: The probabilities of the contacts are calculated from 6000 simulation structures extracted at intervals of 10 ns from the second 0.5 μs of the 120 simulations.
source: The probabilities of the contacts are calculated from 6000 simulation structures extracted at intervals of 10 ns from the second 0.5 μs of the 120 simulations, and indicated in grayscale in Figure 2.
evidence: This claim describes the analysis method for contact probabilities.

claim: Two residues are taken to be in contact in a simulation structure if the minimum distance between non-hydrogen atoms of the residues is smaller than 0.45 nm.
source: As in the contact maps for the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 1, two residues are taken to be in contact in a simulation structure if the minimum distance between non-hydrogen atoms of the residues is smaller than 0.45 nm.
evidence: This claim describes the definition of a contact used in the analysis.

claim: The MD contact maps include the Cα AB loop and the Cβ A and B strand in the constant domains of TCRαβ.
source: Besides the Cα DE loop, Cβ CC' loop, Cβ EF loop, Cβ FG loop, and Cβ G strand with contacts in the cryo-EM structure, the MD contacts maps of Figure 2 include also the Cα AB loop and the Cβ A and B strand in the constant domains of TCRαβ and, remarkably, the three loops A'B, C"D, and EF in the variable region Vα of TCRα.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The MD contact maps include the three loops A'B, C"D, and EF in the variable region Vα of TCRα.
source: Besides the Cα DE loop, Cβ CC' loop, Cβ EF loop, Cβ FG loop, and Cβ G strand with contacts in the cryo-EM structure, the MD contacts maps of Figure 2 include also the Cα AB loop and the Cβ A and B strand in the constant domains of TCRαβ and, remarkably, the three loops A'B, C"D, and EF in the variable region Vα of TCRα.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Residue-residue contacts between Vα and the δ chain of CD3εδ have probabilities smaller than 3%.
source: Residue-residue contacts between Vα and the δ chain of CD3εδ have probabilities smaller than 3%, but occur in 75 of the 120 trajectories and are, thus, a robust feature of our simulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data on contact probabilities.

claim: Residue-residue contacts between Vα and the δ chain of CD3εδ occur in 75 of the 120 trajectories.
source: Residue-residue contacts between Vα and the δ chain of CD3εδ have probabilities smaller than 3%, but occur in 75 of the 120 trajectories and are, thus, a robust feature of our simulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data on contact occurrence.

claim: The tilt angle of TCRαβ EC domain roughly varies between 15° and 55° in the MD simulations.
source: In our MD simulations, the tilt angle of TCRαβ EC domain roughly varies between 15° and 55°, while the rotation angle varies between 0° and 55°.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data on tilt angle distribution.

claim: The rotation angle of TCRαβ EC domain varies between 0° and 55° in the MD simulations.
source: In our MD simulations, the tilt angle of TCRαβ EC domain roughly varies between 15° and 55°, while the rotation angle varies between 0° and 55°.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data on rotation angle distribution.

claim: For tilt angles between 15° and 35°, the rotation angle predominantly adopts values between about 5° and 25°.
source: For tilt angles between 15° and 35°, the rotation angle predominantly adopts values between about 5° and 25°.
evidence: This claim is supported by the two-dimensional probability distribution shown in Figure 3(c).

claim: For a tilt angle of 40°, the most probable value of the rotation angle is about 32°.
source: For a tilt angle of 40°, the most probable value of the rotation angle is about 32°, and further increases to 40° for a tilt angle of 50°.
evidence: This claim is supported by the two-dimensional probability distribution shown in Figure 3(c).

claim: For a tilt angle of 50°, the most probable value of the rotation angle is about 40°.
source: For a tilt angle of 40°, the most probable value of the rotation angle is about 32°, and further increases to 40° for a tilt angle of 50°.
evidence: This claim is supported by the two-dimensional probability distribution shown in Figure 3(c).

claim: The tilt angle for the TCRαβ EC domain in the cryo-EM structure is 31.2±0.4°.
source: From TM domain alignment to the 120 final simulation conformations of our trajectories, we obtain the tilt angle 31.2±0.4° and the rotation angle 14.7±0.7° for the TCRαβ EC domain of the cryo-EM structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural alignment analysis.

claim: The rotation angle for the TCRαβ EC domain in the cryo-EM structure is 14.7±0.7°.
source: From TM domain alignment to the 120 final simulation conformations of our trajectories, we obtain the tilt angle 31.2±0.4° and the rotation angle 14.7±0.7° for the TCRαβ EC domain of the cryo-EM structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural alignment analysis.

claim: Residue-residue contacts of the A'B, C"D, and EF loops of the variable domain Vα with the protein CD3δ only occur for tilt angles of the TCRαβ EC domain larger than about 30°.
source: Residue-residue contacts of the A'B, C"D, and EF loops of the variable domain Vα with the protein CD3δ only occur for tilt angles of the TCRαβ EC domain larger than about 30° (see Figure 3(d)).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3(d).

claim: The average number of Vα-CD3δ residue-residue contacts increases to values around two for tilt angles of 50° and larger.
source: The average number of these residues-residue contacts increases to values around two for tilt angles of 50° and larger.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3(d).

claim: For the Cβ FG loop, the average number of residues-residue contacts decreases from a value around 30 at the tilt angle 15° to values close 0 for tilt angles of 50° and larger.
source: For the Cβ FG loop, in contrast, the average number of residues-residue contacts decreases from a value around 30 at the tilt angle 15° to values close 0 for tilt angles of 50° and larger.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3(d).

claim: The average inclination of the TCRα TM helix relative to the membrane normal decreases from about 11.5° to values around 8.5° with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain.
source: The average inclination of the TCRα TM helix relative to the membrane normal decreases from about 11.5° to values around 8.5° with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain, while the average inclination of the CD3γ TM helix increases from about 15.5° to values around 24° (see Figure 3(e)).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3(e).

claim: The average inclination of the CD3γ TM helix increases from about 15.5° to values around 24° with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain.
source: The average inclination of the TCRα TM helix relative to the membrane normal decreases from about 11.5° to values around 8.5° with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain, while the average inclination of the CD3γ TM helix increases from about 15.5° to values around 24° (see Figure 3(e)).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3(e).

claim: An increased tilt of the TCRαβ EC domain leads to a marked decrease in the contacts between the Cβ FG loop and the CD3εγ EC domain.
source: Our MD simulations show that an increased tilt of the TCRαβ EC domain leads to a marked decrease in the contacts between the Cβ FG loop and the CD3εγ EC domain (see Figure 3(d)), and also to changes in the inclination of TM helices relative to the membrane normal (see Figure 3(e)).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3(d).

claim: An increased tilt of the TCRαβ EC domain leads to changes in the inclination of TM helices relative to the membrane normal.
source: Our MD simulations show that an increased tilt of the TCRαβ EC domain leads to a marked decrease in the contacts between the Cβ FG loop and the CD3εγ EC domain (see Figure 3(d)), and also to changes in the inclination of TM helices relative to the membrane normal (see Figure 3(e)).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3(e).

claim: Structural changes in the TM domain of the TCR – CD3 have been suggested to be involved in the transmission of forces from the EC domain to the signaling motifs on the intracellular segments of the CD3 chains.
source: Such structural changes in the TM domain of the TCR – CD3 have been suggested to be involved in the transmission of forces from the EC domain to the signaling motifs on the intracellular segments of the CD3 chains (Brazin et al., 2015; Brazin et al., 2018), which are not resolved in the cryo-EM structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brazin et al., 2015 and Brazin et al., 2018.

claim: The intracellular segments of the CD3 chains are not resolved in the cryo-EM structure.
source: Such structural changes in the TM domain of the TCR – CD3 have been suggested to be involved in the transmission of forces from the EC domain to the signaling motifs on the intracellular segments of the CD3 chains (Brazin et al., 2015; Brazin et al., 2018), which are not resolved in the cryo-EM structure.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The Cα AB loop has been implicated in TCR triggering.
source: Similar to the Cβ FG loop, we also find a decrease of contacts between the Cα AB loop, which has been implicated in TCR triggering (Beddoe et al., 2009), and the ε chain of the CD3εγ EC domain with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beddoe et al., 2009.

claim: There is a decrease of contacts between the Cα AB loop and the ε chain of the CD3εγ EC domain with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain.
source: Similar to the Cβ FG loop, we also find a decrease of contacts between the Cα AB loop, which has been implicated in TCR triggering (Beddoe et al., 2009), and the ε chain of the CD3εγ EC domain with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MHC class I and MHC class II EC domains are anchored by one and two peptide linkers, respectively, to a pair of transmembrane helices.
source: This assumption appears reasonable because MHC class I and MHC class II EC domains are anchored by one and two peptide linkers, respectively, to a pair of transmembrane helices, whereas the three EC domains of the TCR - CD3 complex are jointly anchored by six linkers to a bundle of eight transmembrane helices.
evidence: This claim is based on established structural knowledge of MHC molecules.

claim: The three EC domains of the TCR - CD3 complex are jointly anchored by six linkers to a bundle of eight transmembrane helices.
source: This assumption appears reasonable because MHC class I and MHC class II EC domains are anchored by one and two peptide linkers, respectively, to a pair of transmembrane helices, whereas the three EC domains of the TCR - CD3 complex are jointly anchored by six linkers to a bundle of eight transmembrane helices.
evidence: This claim is based on the cryo-EM structure and simulation setup.

claim: A presumably binding-incompetent, supine conformation of MHC class I molecules was observed in two-dimensional crystals in which the MHC EC domains are positioned with their 'sides' on the membrane.
source: The anchoring flexibility of MHC class I molecules is also illustrated by a presumably binding-incompetent, supine conformation observed in two-dimensional crystals in which the MHC EC domains are positioned with their 'sides' on the membrane, rather than 'standing up' (Mitra et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mitra et al., 2004.

claim: Transversal forces on TCR-MHC complexes up to 5 pN are within the range measured with force sensors.
source: Such transversal forces on TCR-MHC complexes up to 5 pN are within the range measured with force sensors (Göhring et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Göhring et al., 2020.

claim: In the kinetic segregation mechanism, a key step in T cell activation is the size-based segregation of the inhibitory tyrosine phosphatase CD45 from TCR-MHC complexes.
source: In the kinetic segregation mechanism, a key step in T cell activation is the size-based segregation of the inhibitory tyrosine phosphatase CD45 from TCR-MHC complexes (Davis and van der Merwe, 2006; Choudhuri and van der Merwe, 2007; Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on the kinetic segregation mechanism.

claim: CD2-CD58 complexes segregate from TCR-MHC complexes.
source: Such force-induced decreases of the membrane separation at the site of TCR-MHC complexes may also be relevant for the the recently observed segregation of CD2-CD58 complexes from TCR-MHC complexes, which both have EC domain lengths of about 13 nm (Demetriou et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Demetriou et al., 2019.

claim: CD2-CD58 complexes and TCR-MHC complexes both have EC domain lengths of about 13 nm.
source: Such force-induced decreases of the membrane separation at the site of TCR-MHC complexes may also be relevant for the the recently observed segregation of CD2-CD58 complexes from TCR-MHC complexes, which both have EC domain lengths of about 13 nm (Demetriou et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Demetriou et al., 2019.

claim: The orientations of the TCRαβ EC domain within the TCR – CD3 complex are affected by the low-affinity interactions with the CD3εγ and CD3εδ EC domains.
source: The orientations of the TCRαβ EC domain within the TCR – CD3 complex are affected by the low-affinity interactions with the CD3εγ and CD3εδ EC domains (He et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He et al., 2015.

claim: Coarse-grained models have inherent limitations in describing low-affinity interactions.
source: Because of the inherent limitations of coarse-grained models to describe such low-affinity interactions (Javanainen et al., 2017), we chose state-of-the-art atomistic force fields for our simulations of the TCR – CD3 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Javanainen et al., 2017.

claim: The 120 simulation trajectories with a length of 1 μs provide a cumulative sampling on timescales that exceed the length of the individual trajectories.
source: Our 120 simulation trajectories with a length of 1 μs provide a cumulative sampling on timescales that exceed the length of the individual trajectories (Pande et al., 2003; Noé et al., 2009) and lead to equilibrated conformational and orientational distributions of the EC domains (see Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pande et al., 2003 and Noé et al., 2009 about cumulative sampling.

claim: The TCRα TM helix remains intact on the microsecond timescales of the simulations and does not break into two helix halves connected by a hinge.
source: The TCRα TM helix remains intact on the microsecond timescales of our simulations and does not break into two helix halves connected by a hinge.
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from the simulation data.

claim: Bending of the TCRα TM helix at a helix hinge was observed in NMR experiments.
source: Larger conformational rearrangements of the TM helices such as the bending of the TCRα TM helix at a helix hinge observed in NMR experiments (Brazin et al., 2018) may occur on longer timescales, and may also depend on the composition of the lipid membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brazin et al., 2018.

claim: Larger conformational rearrangements of the TM helices may occur on longer timescales than those simulated.
source: Larger conformational rearrangements of the TM helices such as the bending of the TCRα TM helix at a helix hinge observed in NMR experiments (Brazin et al., 2018) may occur on longer timescales, and may also depend on the composition of the lipid membrane.
evidence: This is a speculation about processes beyond the simulation timescale.

claim: Conformational rearrangements of the TM helices may depend on the composition of the lipid membrane.
source: Larger conformational rearrangements of the TM helices such as the bending of the TCRα TM helix at a helix hinge observed in NMR experiments (Brazin et al., 2018) may occur on longer timescales, and may also depend on the composition of the lipid membrane.
evidence: This is a speculation about factors affecting TM helix conformations.

claim: Coarse-grained force fields have limitations in modeling secondary structure propensities and disordered protein segments.
source: How these orientational changes are affected by the membrane composition, and whether they can be related to conformational changes in the largely disordered intracellular signaling domains requires further simulations, likely with atomistic resolution because of limitations in modeling secondary structure propensities and disordered protein segments with coarse-grained force fields (Monticelli et al., 2008; Robustelli et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Monticelli et al., 2008 and Robustelli et al., 2018.

claim: Recent modeling based on the cryo-EM structure included the intracellular signaling domains in coarse-grained simulations of the entire complex with a cumulative simulation time of 25 μs.
source: In recent modeling based on the cryo-EM structure of the TCR – CD3 complex, the intracellular signaling domains have been included in coarse-grained simulations of the entire complex with a cumulative simulation time of 25 μs (Prakaash et al., 2021), and the conformations of the TM domain in a complex, asymmetric membrane have been explored in atomistic simulations with a cumulative simulation time of about 4 μs (Lanz et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Prakaash et al., 2021.

claim: The conformations of the TM domain in a complex, asymmetric membrane have been explored in atomistic simulations with a cumulative simulation time of about 4 μs.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lanz et al., 2021.

claim: The production simulations used a Langevin thermostat with a Langevin collision frequency of 1.0 ps-1.
source: We used a Langevin thermostat with a Langevin collision frequency of 1.0 ps-1, and the Berendsen barostat with semi-isotropic pressure coupling and a relaxation time of 1 ps to apply a constant pressure of 1 bar in all directions at which the membrane is tensionless.
evidence: This claim describes the simulation parameters.

claim: The production simulations used the Berendsen barostat with semi-isotropic pressure coupling and a relaxation time of 1 ps.
source: We used a Langevin thermostat with a Langevin collision frequency of 1.0 ps-1, and the Berendsen barostat with semi-isotropic pressure coupling and a relaxation time of 1 ps to apply a constant pressure of 1 bar in all directions at which the membrane is tensionless.
evidence: This claim describes the simulation parameters.

source: In addition, we applied hydrogen mass repartitioning (Hopkins et al., 2015) to all the hydrogen atoms on protein and lipids in the production simulations, which allowed to increase to the MD integration time step to 4 fs.
evidence: This claim describes the simulation parameters.

claim: Hydrogen mass repartitioning allowed to increase the MD integration time step to 4 fs.

claim: The tilt angle distribution of the equilibrated ensemble of 6000 simulation structures has a mean of 33.4° and a standard deviation of 8.9°.
source: The tilt angle distribution of the equilibrated ensemble of 6000 simulation structures has a mean of 33.4° and a standard deviation of 8.9°, the rotation angle distributions has a mean of 26.1° and a standard deviation of 15.1°, while the distribution of the angle between axis A and B of the TCRαβ EC domain has a mean of 86.5° and a significantly smaller standard deviation of 1.9°.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of simulation data.

claim: The rotation angle distribution has a mean of 26.1° and a standard deviation of 15.1°.
source: The tilt angle distribution of the equilibrated ensemble of 6000 simulation structures has a mean of 33.4° and a standard deviation of 8.9°, the rotation angle distributions has a mean of 26.1° and a standard deviation of 15.1°, while the distribution of the angle between axis A and B of the TCRαβ EC domain has a mean of 86.5° and a significantly smaller standard deviation of 1.9°.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of simulation data.

claim: The distribution of the angle between axis A and B of the TCRαβ EC domain has a mean of 86.5° and a standard deviation of 1.9°.
source: The tilt angle distribution of the equilibrated ensemble of 6000 simulation structures has a mean of 33.4° and a standard deviation of 8.9°, the rotation angle distributions has a mean of 26.1° and a standard deviation of 15.1°, while the distribution of the angle between axis A and B of the TCRαβ EC domain has a mean of 86.5° and a significantly smaller standard deviation of 1.9°.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of simulation data.

claim: The small standard deviation of the angle between axes A and B indicates that the large TCRαβ EC domain can be seen as rather stable and rigid within the TCR - CD3 complex.
source: This small standard deviation indicates that the large TCRαβ EC domain can be seen as rather stable and rigid within the TCR - CD3 complex, which is supported by the small average root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of about 2 Å for the Cα atoms of the TCRαβ EC domain simulation structures relative to the cryo-EM structure (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the statistical analysis of simulation data.

claim: The average root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) is about 2 Å for the Cα atoms of the TCRαβ EC domain simulation structures relative to the cryo-EM structure.
source: This small standard deviation indicates that the large TCRαβ EC domain can be seen as rather stable and rigid within the TCR - CD3 complex, which is supported by the small average root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of about 2 Å for the Cα atoms of the TCRαβ EC domain simulation structures relative to the cryo-EM structure (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RMSD analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average Cα RMSDs of the CD3εδ and CD3εγ EC domains relative to the cryo-EM structure are only slightly larger than those of TCRαβ.
source: The average Cα RMSDs of the CD3εδ and CD3εγ EC domains relatively to the cryo-EM structure are only slightly larger and exhibit a marginal increase of about 0.3 Å along the second trajectory halves.
evidence: This claim is supported by RMSD analysis of simulation data.

claim: The average Cα RMSDs of the CD3εδ and CD3εγ EC domains exhibit a marginal increase of about 0.3 Å along the second trajectory halves.
source: The average Cα RMSDs of the CD3εδ and CD3εγ EC domains relatively to the cryo-EM structure are only slightly larger and exhibit a marginal increase of about 0.3 Å along the second trajectory halves.
evidence: This claim is supported by RMSD analysis of simulation data.

claim: The three EC domains of the TCR - CD3 complex are rather stable.
source: Overall, these RMSDs and the small variations of the angle between axis A and B of the TCRαβ EC domain indicate that the three EC domains of the TCR - CD3 complex are rather stable.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from RMSD and angle variation analysis.

claim: The main structural variations of the complex arise from the orientational variations of TCRαβ EC domain relative to the membrane.
source: The main structural variations of the complex arise from the orientational variations of TCRαβ EC domain relative to the membrane, which are associated with the characteristic changes in the quaternary interactions between the EC domains illustrated in Figure 3.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the simulation data analysis.

claim: The membrane thickness does not change with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain within the statistical accuracy.
source: Within the statistical accuracy, the membrane thickness does not change with increasing tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane thickness analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3(b).

claim: The largest positive correlations of clusters in the TCRαβ/CD3εδ contact map occur between the contact clusters 1 to 4.
source: The largest positive correlations of clusters in the TCRαβ/CD3εδ contact map of Figure 2 occur between the contact clusters 1 to 4 (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1, top left), which correspond to interactions of the variable domain Vα of TCRα and the δ chain of CD3εδ.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Contact clusters 1 to 4 correspond to interactions of the variable domain Vα of TCRα and the δ chain of CD3εδ.
source: The largest positive correlations of clusters in the TCRαβ/CD3εδ contact map of Figure 2 occur between the contact clusters 1 to 4 (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1, top left), which correspond to interactions of the variable domain Vα of TCRα and the δ chain of CD3εδ.
evidence: This claim is supported by the contact map analysis in Figure 2.

claim: The large positive correlations of contact clusters 1 to 4 can be understood from the coupling to the tilt of the TCRαβ EC domain.
source: The large positive correlations of these four contact clusters can be understood from the coupling to the tilt of the TCRαβ EC domain, because the contacts of the Vα domain reported by the four contact clusters are only possible at high tilt angles of the TCRαβ EC domain (see Figure 3(d)).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation and tilt angle analysis.

claim: Relatively large positive correlations occur between the clusters 13 to 21 of the TCRαβ/CD3εγ contact map.
source: Relatively large positive correlations occur also between the clusters 13 to 21 of the TCRαβ/CD3εγ contact map (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1, bottom left).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overall weak correlations between the majority of the other contact clusters indicate independent motions of the loops and strands involved in these EC domain contacts.
source: Besides these positive correlations that result from the concerted conformational changes coupled to the tilt angle of the TCRαβ EC domain, the overall weak correlations between the majority of the other contact clusters in Figure 2 indicate independent motions of the loops and strands involved in these EC domain contacts.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation analysis.

claim: Relatively strongly negative correlations of several pairs of contact clusters point to alternative EC domain contacts.
source: In addition, relatively strongly negative correlations of several pairs of contact clusters point to alternative EC domain contacts.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation analysis.

claim: The overall rather negative correlations between the clusters 13 to 21 and the cluster 22 show that the interaction of the Cβ G strand and the γ AB loop is not compatible with the interactions of the Cβ FG loop and G strand to the ε chain and the N-terminus of the γ chain of CD3εγ.
source: For example, the overall rather negative correlations between the clusters 13 to 21 and the cluster 22 of the TCRαβ/CD3εγ contact map show that the interaction of the Cβ G strand and the γ AB loop reported by cluster 22 is not compatible with the interactions of the Cβ FG loop and G strand to the ε chain and the N-terminus of the γ chain of CD3εγ, which are reflected by the clusters 13 to 21.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation analysis.

claim: The orientation of the TCR EC domain relative to the membrane is coupled to structural changes throughout the TCR – CD3 complex.
source: Overall, our simulations reveal that the orientation of the TCR EC domain relative to the membrane is coupled to structural changes throughout the TCR – CD3 complex.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding from the simulation data.

claim: The overall weak correlations of the majority of EC domain interactions indicate additional independent motions of the loops and strands that are involved in these interactions.
source: Besides this concerted structural motion, the overall weak correlations of the majority of EC domain interactions indicate additional independent motions of the loops and strands that are involved in these interactions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation analysis.
